This page is an explanation, not the original paper.

This is an exposition of my paper Geometry of Geometric Data Set II: Pyramid, arXiv:2603.23325v3 (revised March 28, 2026). It covers the compactification of a class of geometric data sets (GDSs) by pyramids (Proposition 7.3) and the limit formula for observable diameter that holds on it (Corollary 7.7). Theorem and lemma numbers follow the HTML version of the fixed version v3. Theorem 1.1, Proposition 1.2 and Corollary 1.3 of the introduction are Theorem 4.10, Proposition 7.3 and Corollary 7.7 of the body. Versions v1 and v2 are organized into sections differently and give the same theorems other numbers (completeness and separability is Theorem 5.9 there), so please do not mix versions when citing. Prior work is used only when the paper cites it directly.

I assume the basics of metric spaces and Borel probability measures: completeness, separability, push-forward measures and 1-Lipschitz functions. The results of the previous paper on GDSs (GDS I, arXiv:2603.23316, reference [9] of the paper) and the technical part of Section 6 of v3 (the stair space) are used as background results: I state their conclusions and do not reproduce their proofs.

Boxed theorems are claims of the paper. Paragraphs beginning "Explainer's note." and the items labelled "Explainer's example" are my additions for readability and are not statements of the paper. Where the paper's text had a defect that I repaired, the passage is marked "Distinction from the source." Definitions in detail and long verifications are placed in expandable blocks.

Question | Can collecting observations give a limit to a sequence of data that does not converge?

The idea of a GDS is to represent data as a set of points together with a family of real-valued functions (features) that measure those points. Closeness of points is decided by the discrepancy of feature values. A sequence of data sets need not converge to a single GDS. For example, the sequence of two-point GDSs at distance nnn, carrying all 1-Lipschitz functions, does not concentrate to any GDS as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞ (checked by an example in the compactification section).

So we want to take, for each term of the sequence, the object consisting of all observations that can be extracted from it. Can the sequence of such "collections of observations" be given a limit even when the original sequence does not converge? And can a statistic such as the observable diameter then be read off from that limit?

The paper's answer has three steps.

  1. Fix a family L\mathcal LL of allowed processings of features (a family of 1-Lipschitz functions on the real line), and work only with GDSs whose features can be bundled into finitely many representatives by L\mathcal LL. This class D/L\mathcal D/\mathcal LD/L is complete and separable in box distance (Theorem 4.10).
  2. When L\mathcal LL contains translations and clippings, the space ΠL\Pi_{\mathcal L}ΠL​ of all collections of observations (pyramids) is a compactification of D/L\mathcal D/\mathcal LD/L with respect to the observable distance dconcd_{\mathrm{conc}}dconc​ (Proposition 7.3).
  3. When L\mathcal LL is the family of all 1-Lipschitz functions, a limit formula holds for the observable diameter of pyramids (Corollary 7.7).

The rest of this page proceeds as follows. We first fix GDSs and the two distances, and see how a free family of features destroys separability. Then we introduce finite approximation by the family of processings L\mathcal LL and prove completeness and separability. After that we define pyramids and treat, in order, the compactification, the limit formula for observable diameter, and an application to data whose features are distance functions.

Object | A GDS is a set of points with a family of features, compared by two distances

The "data" and the "closeness" in the question are fixed here by definitions.

GDS. A GDS is a triple X=(X,FX,μX)X=(X,F_X,\mu_X)X=(X,FX​,μX​). Here FXF_XFX​ is a nonempty family of real-valued functions on XXX such that

dX(x,y)=sup⁡f∈FX∣f(x)−f(y)∣ d_X(x,y)=\sup_{f\in F_X}|f(x)-f(y)| dX​(x,y)=f∈FX​sup​∣f(x)−f(y)∣

is a complete separable metric, and μX\mu_XμX​ is a Borel probability measure of full support on (X,dX)(X,d_X)(X,dX​). Full support means that every nonempty open set has positive probability. Every f∈FXf\in F_Xf∈FX​ is 1-Lipschitz with respect to dXd_XdX​. If we take FX=Lip⁡1(X,dX)F_X=\operatorname{Lip}_1(X,d_X)FX​=Lip1​(X,dX​), the functions f=dX(⋅,y)f=d_X(\cdot,y)f=dX​(⋅,y) recover the original metric, so ordinary mm-spaces (a complete separable metric space with a Borel probability measure of full support) are included as a special case (Definition 2.13 and the introduction; the definition is due to Hanika–Schneider–Stumme [4]).

Explainer's note. Closeness of points can be measured only through feature values. The same point set with a different family of features receives a different metric. In this sense, "which functions we use to observe the points" is part of the geometry of the data.

Write F‾\overline FF for the closure of a feature family FFF under pointwise convergence. For 1-Lipschitz families it coincides with the closure under convergence in probability (Lemma 2.5, [9]). One shared exceptional set (box distance). The box distance □\Box□ can be written as

□(X,Y)=min⁡π, Smax⁡{1−π(S), 2(d∞S)H(FX‾∘pr1, FY‾∘pr2)} \Box(X,Y)=\min_{\pi,\ S}\max\Bigl\{1-\pi(S),\ 2(d^S_\infty)_H\bigl(\overline{F_X}\circ\mathrm{pr}_1,\ \overline{F_Y}\circ\mathrm{pr}_2\bigr)\Bigr\} □(X,Y)=π, Smin​max{1−π(S), 2(d∞S​)H​(FX​​∘pr1​, FY​​∘pr2​)}

Explainer's note. In the observable distance, each feature may use its own exceptional set. In the box distance, all features must share one exceptional set SSS. This makes □\Box□ a stronger distance than dconcd_{\mathrm{conc}}dconc​. The goal of the paper is a compactification for dconcd_{\mathrm{conc}}dconc​; □\Box□ is the stage on which we take limits in a complete separable space, and a tool for the proofs.

Obstacle | If the feature family is free, countably many samples cannot approximate it

Both distances are now in place. A compact metric space is separable, so before building any compactification we need at least separability. But the abstract of the paper states that on all of D\mathcal DD the distance dconcd_{\mathrm{conc}}dconc​ is not separable, and that □\Box□ is complete but not separable (non-separability is shown in [9]).

Explainer's example. This phenomenon already occurs for GDSs with a single point. On a one-point set {∗}\{*\}{∗} a feature is just a real number, so for every nonempty A⊂RA\subset\mathbb RA⊂R the triple ({∗},A,δ∗)(\{*\},A,\delta_*)({∗},A,δ∗​) is a GDS. Its isomorphism class is determined by the closure of AAA in R\mathbb RR. The Ky Fan distance on a one-point space is dKF(a,b)=min⁡{∣a−b∣,1}d_{\mathrm{KF}}(a,b)=\min\{|a-b|,1\}dKF​(a,b)=min{∣a−b∣,1}, so dconcd_{\mathrm{conc}}dconc​ is the Hausdorff distance between closed sets measured with this truncated distance.

Let A,BA,BA,B be distinct nonempty subsets of Z\mathbb ZZ. Choose n∈A∖Bn\in A\setminus Bn∈A∖B. Every element of BBB is at distance at least 1 from nnn, so dconc(A,B)=1d_{\mathrm{conc}}(A,B)=1dconc​(A,B)=1 (the Ky Fan distance never exceeds 1). There are continuum many subsets of Z\mathbb ZZ, any two at distance 1, so there is no countable dense subset. Since □≥dconc\Box\geq d_{\mathrm{conc}}□≥dconc​, the same holds for □\Box□.

The cause is that the feature families cannot be bundled together. In the next section we allow "processing" of features and gather features that are carried to each other by processing under one representative.

Tool | Allow processing of features and approximate a feature family by finitely many representatives

In the one-point example the subsets AAA of Z\mathbb ZZ stayed apart and never mixed. If we allowed adding a real number to each feature and regarded the results as the same, every AAA would collapse to all of R\mathbb RR. The family L\mathcal LL of processings generalizes this idea.

Let Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R) be the family of all 1-Lipschitz functions on the real line. A subfamily L⊂Lip⁡1(R)\mathcal L\subset\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)L⊂Lip1​(R) is monoidal if it contains the identity idR\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R}idR​ and is closed under composition and under pointwise convergence on R\mathbb RR (Definition 3.1). The following families are examples (Definition 3.2).

  • T={t↦t+c∣c∈R}\mathcal T=\{t\mapsto t+c\mid c\in\mathbb R\}T={t↦t+c∣c∈R}: translations.
  • B={bR∣R∈[0,+∞]}\mathcal B=\{b_R\mid R\in[0,+\infty]\}B={bR​∣R∈[0,+∞]}, bR(t)=max⁡{−R,min⁡{t,R}}b_R(t)=\max\{-R,\min\{t,R\}\}bR​(t)=max{−R,min{t,R}}: clippings.
  • TB={t↦max⁡{l,min⁡{t+c,u}}∣c∈R, l∈[−∞,+∞), u∈(−∞,+∞], l≤u}\mathcal{TB}=\{t\mapsto\max\{l,\min\{t+c,u\}\}\mid c\in\mathbb R,\ l\in[-\infty,+\infty),\ u\in(-\infty,+\infty],\ l\leq u\}TB={t↦max{l,min{t+c,u}}∣c∈R, l∈[−∞,+∞), u∈(−∞,+∞], l≤u}: the smallest monoidal family containing both.
  • The whole of Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R).

For a subfamily F⊂FX‾F\subset\overline{F_X}F⊂FX​​ of a GDS XXX, write L∘F={p∘f∣p∈L, f∈F}\mathcal L\circ F=\{p\circ f\mid p\in\mathcal L,\ f\in F\}L∘F={p∘f∣p∈L, f∈F}. The family FFF is L\mathcal LL-closed if L∘F⊂F\mathcal L\circ F\subset FL∘F⊂F. The (ε,L)(\varepsilon,\mathcal L)(ε,L)-covering number is

cov⁡(F,ε;L)=inf⁡{#N∣N⊂F is finite, F⊂U(L∘N,ε;dKFX)}, \operatorname{cov}(F,\varepsilon;\mathcal L)=\inf\{\#\mathcal N\mid\mathcal N\subset F\text{ is finite},\ F\subset U(\mathcal L\circ\mathcal N,\varepsilon;d_{\mathrm{KF}}^X)\}, cov(F,ε;L)=inf{#N∣N⊂F is finite, F⊂U(L∘N,ε;dKFX​)},

where U(⋅,ε;d)U(\cdot,\varepsilon;d)U(⋅,ε;d) is the open ε\varepsilonε-neighbourhood with respect to ddd. The family FFF is L\mathcal LL-compact if it is L\mathcal LL-closed and the covering number is finite for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0. A GDS XXX is L\mathcal LL-compact if FX‾\overline{F_X}FX​​ is L\mathcal LL-compact. Write D/L\mathcal D/\mathcal LD/L for the set of isomorphism classes of such GDSs (Definitions 3.3, 3.5, 3.8). This notation names a class; it is not a definition identifying GDSs under processing.

Explainer's note. L\mathcal LL-compactness says that the feature family can be bundled into finitely many representatives "up to a change of scale by L\mathcal LL". We regard fff and p∘fp\circ fp∘f (p∈Lp\in\mathcal Lp∈L) as the same observation on different scales and gather them near one representative.

Back to the example of the obstacle. Suppose a one-point GDS ({∗},A,δ∗)(\{*\},A,\delta_*)({∗},A,δ∗​) is L\mathcal LL-closed and T⊂L\mathcal T\subset\mathcal LT⊂L. Translating any a∈Aa\in Aa∈A produces every real number, so A=RA=\mathbb RA=R. This one-point GDS with A=RA=\mathbb RA=R is T\mathcal TT-compact, because the single constant 000 serves as the representative. If only {idR}\{\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R}\}{idR​} is allowed, this constant feature family is not totally bounded in dKFd_{\mathrm{KF}}dKF​, hence not {idR}\{\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R}\}{idR​}-compact (Remark 3.6). "Compact" here does not mean ordinary compactness of the feature family itself; it means approximability using the allowed processings.

For families containing translations, the second condition of L\mathcal LL-compactness holds automatically.

Theorem 3.19. Let L⊃T\mathcal L\supset\mathcal TL⊃T and let XXX be a GDS. If a subfamily FFF of FXF_XFX​ is L\mathcal LL-closed, then FFF is L\mathcal LL-compact.

Consequently, for example, the GDS obtained from an mm-space by taking all 1-Lipschitz functions as features is Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R)-compact (Corollary 3.20). In the proof, translations that align the values at one point realize the approximation by finitely many representatives.

One more property of the class D/L\mathcal D/\mathcal LD/L is needed. If a sequence XnX_nXn​ of L\mathcal LL-compact GDSs concentrates to XXX, then XXX is also L\mathcal LL-compact (Proposition 3.7). Together with dconc≤□d_{\mathrm{conc}}\leq\Boxdconc​≤□ and the completeness of (D,□)(\mathcal D,\Box)(D,□), this shows that D/L\mathcal D/\mathcal LD/L is closed in □\Box□ and complete with respect to □\Box□ (Remark 3.9).

Result | The class of GDSs approximable by finitely many representatives is complete and separable in box distance

The previous section defined L\mathcal LL-compactness. Theorem 4.10 answers whether this condition removes the non-separability seen in the obstacle.

Theorem 4.10. For every monoidal family L\mathcal LL, (D/L,□)(\mathcal D/\mathcal L,\Box)(D/L,□) is complete and separable.

Beyond being monoidal, L\mathcal LL carries no assumption, so the theorem applies to each of {idR}\{\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R}\}{idR​}, T\mathcal TT, TB\mathcal{TB}TB and Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R). Complete means that Cauchy sequences have limits in the class; separable means that countably many GDSs approximate the whole class to any precision.

This theorem is used directly when we deal with pyramids. In a complete separable metric space, a sequence of closed sets has a weakly convergent subsequence (Lemma 2.11, Beer [1]). Pyramids are treated as closed sets of (D/L,□)(\mathcal D/\mathcal L,\Box)(D/L,□), and this lemma guarantees the existence of limits.

Proof | Completeness follows from closedness; separability from approximation by bounded GDSs with finitely many features

Theorem 4.10 makes two claims. Completeness follows from the fact that D/L\mathcal D/\mathcal LD/L is a closed subset of the complete space (D,□)(\mathcal D,\Box)(D,□) (Remark 3.9). For separability, we approximate each GDS by a GDS with finitely many features whose values lie in a bounded range.

The picture of a cube. Write DM(N,R)\mathcal{DM}(N,R)DM(N,R) for the set of all GDSs with at most NNN features, all of whose values lie in [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] (Definition 4.3). If FX={f1,…,fN}F_X=\{f_1,\ldots,f_N\}FX​={f1​,…,fN​}, then

x⟼(f1(x),…,fN(x))∈[−R,R]N x\longmapsto(f_1(x),\ldots,f_N(x))\in[-R,R]^N x⟼(f1​(x),…,fN​(x))∈[−R,R]N

is an isometry from dXd_XdX​ to the ℓ∞\ell^\inftyℓ∞ distance of the cube, and each feature becomes a coordinate projection. So such a GDS is the same thing as (the support of) a probability measure on the cube. The proof of Lemma 4.5 uses this correspondence and shows that measures at Prokhorov distance less than ε\varepsilonε are at □\Box□-distance at most 2ε2\varepsilon2ε. The set of probability measures on a cube is compact in dPd_{\mathrm{P}}dP​, so DM(N,R)\mathcal{DM}(N,R)DM(N,R) is compact in □\Box□. The processed family L∘DM(N,R)\mathcal L\circ\mathcal{DM}(N,R)L∘DM(N,R) is compact as well (Lemmas 4.5 and 4.6).

Approximation. We approximate an arbitrary L\mathcal LL-compact GDS XXX by this family of cubes. Choose a compact set K⊂XK\subset XK⊂X with probability >1−ε>1-\varepsilon>1−ε. Lemma 2.8 says that if two 1-Lipschitz functions are close in Ky Fan distance, then they are uniformly close on KKK. The finitely many representatives N\mathcal NN given by L\mathcal LL-compactness approximate all features in Ky Fan distance, hence uniformly on KKK. Each representative is bounded on KKK, so for some RRR its values on KKK lie in [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] (Lemma 4.8). Moreover, clipping the representatives by bRb_RbR​ changes nothing on KKK. The quotient GDS that keeps only the clipped representatives as features is an element of DM(N,R)\mathcal{DM}(N,R)DM(N,R), and its processing by L\mathcal LL approximates XXX within 2ε2\varepsilon2ε in □\Box□ (Lemma 4.9).

The estimate in Lemma 4.9: □(X,L∘Y)<2ε\Box\bigl(X,\mathcal L\circ Y\bigr)<2\varepsilon□(X,L∘Y)<2ε

  1. #N≤N\#\mathcal N\leq N#N≤N.
  2. μX(S)>1−ε\mu_X(S)>1-\varepsilonμX​(S)>1−ε.
  3. FX⊂U(L∘N,ε;d∞S)F_X\subset U(\mathcal L\circ\mathcal N,\varepsilon;d^S_\infty)FX​⊂U(L∘N,ε;d∞S​).
  4. sup⁡{∣f(x)∣∣f∈N, x∈S}≤R\sup\{|f(x)|\mid f\in\mathcal N,\ x\in S\}\leq Rsup{∣f(x)∣∣f∈N, x∈S}≤R.

Lemma 4.8 says that for an L\mathcal LL-compact XXX and ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 there are N,RN,RN,R with X∈DM(N,R;L,ε)X\in\mathcal{DM}(N,R;\mathcal L,\varepsilon)X∈DM(N,R;L,ε). In Lemma 4.9, let YYY be the quotient GDS of XXX keeping only the features bR∘Nb_R\circ\mathcal NbR​∘N. Limit space | A pyramid is the closed set of all observations visible beneath a GDS

By Theorem 4.10, (D/L,□)(\mathcal D/\mathcal L,\Box)(D/L,□) is a complete separable space. A sequence in this space still need not converge in D/L\mathcal D/\mathcal LD/L (an example in the next section checks this). So instead of the GDS XXX itself, we take as the new point the totality of observations visible beneath XXX. This section introduces its definition.

Domination and pyramids. For GDSs Y,XY,XY,X, we say that XXX dominates YYY, and write Y⪯XY\preceq XY⪯X, if there is a distribution-preserving Borel map φ ⁣:X→Y\varphi\colon X\to Yφ:X→Y with FY∘φ⊂FX‾F_Y\circ\varphi\subset\overline{F_X}FY​∘φ⊂FX​​ (Definition 2.14). For X∈D/LX\in\mathcal D/\mathcal LX∈D/L put PX={Y∈D/L∣Y⪯X}\mathcal P_X=\{Y\in\mathcal D/\mathcal L\mid Y\preceq X\}PX​={Y∈D/L∣Y⪯X} (Definition 5.2). In general, a subset P⊂D/L\mathcal P\subset\mathcal D/\mathcal LP⊂D/L is an L\mathcal LL-pyramid if it satisfies the following three conditions (Definition 5.1).

  1. If X∈D/LX\in\mathcal D/\mathcal LX∈D/L, Y∈PY\in\mathcal PY∈P and X⪯YX\preceq YX⪯Y, then X∈PX\in\mathcal PX∈P.

  3. P\mathcal PP is nonempty and □\Box□-closed.

Write ΠL\Pi_{\mathcal L}ΠL​ for the set of all L\mathcal LL-pyramids. That PX\mathcal P_XPX​ is an L\mathcal LL-pyramid follows from the property that domination is preserved under limits (Theorem 2.18; Remark 5.3).

Explainer's note. For G⊂FX‾G\subset\overline{F_X}G⊂FX​​, the quotient GDS X/GX/GX/G keeps only the features GGG and identifies points that GGG cannot distinguish (Definition 2.15; existence is from [9]). Since X/G⪯XX/G\preceq XX/G⪯X, the set PX\mathcal P_XPX​ contains every L\mathcal LL-compact GDS obtained from XXX by dropping features or by coarsening through identification of points. The three conditions ask that an observation of an observation is again an observation (1), that two observations can be handled beneath common data (2), and that limits of approximations are included (3).

(Definition 2.10). Points of the limit can be approximated, and points outside it cannot be approached. Finitely many bounded observations. To replace weak convergence by a more manageable distance, we use observations cut out by finitely many features. Let DM(X;N)\mathcal{DM}(X;N)DM(X;N) be the set of GDSs YYY with at most NNN features and Y⪯XY\preceq XY⪯X, and let DM(X;N,R)\mathcal{DM}(X;N,R)DM(X;N,R) be the set of GDSs obtained from them by clipping the features with bRb_RbR​. Proof | The limit is a pyramid, closeness of observations is preserved, and the image is dense

Proposition 7.3 asserts four things: that ρ\rhoρ is a metric, compactness, embedding and density. We follow the mechanism of each proof in turn.

ρ\rhoρ is a metric. If ρ(P,Q)=0\rho(\mathcal P,\mathcal Q)=0ρ(P,Q)=0, then □H(DM(P;N,N),DM(Q;N,N))=0\Box_H(\mathcal{DM}(\mathcal P;N,N),\mathcal{DM}(\mathcal Q;N,N))=0□H​(DM(P;N,N),DM(Q;N,N))=0 for each NNN, so by Proposition 7.2(3) the constant sequence Pn=P\mathcal P_n=\mathcal PPn​=P converges weakly to Q\mathcal QQ. By Proposition 7.2 weak convergence is the same as convergence in ρ\rhoρ, so it suffices to show that the limit P\mathcal PP is a nonempty L\mathcal LL-pyramid. We use the self-compactness of L\mathcal LL that follows from T⊂L\mathcal T\subset\mathcal LT⊂L (Proposition 3.14).

  2. Condition 2 (existence of an upper bound). Take approximations Xn,Yn∈PnX_n,Y_n\in\mathcal P_nXn​,Yn​∈Pn​ of X,Y∈PX,Y\in\mathcal PX,Y∈P, and an upper bound Zˉn\bar Z_nZˉn​ in Pn\mathcal P_nPn​. Lemma 5.5 replaces it by ZnZ_nZn​ with Xn,Yn⪯Zn⪯ZˉnX_n,Y_n\preceq Z_n\preceq\bar Z_nXn​,Yn​⪯Zn​⪯Zˉn​ whose complexity is controlled (in DM(N,R;L,ε)\mathcal{DM}(N,R;\mathcal L,\varepsilon)DM(N,R;L,ε), NNN is doubled and ε\varepsilonε is at most doubled). The resulting observation YnY_nYn​ lies in Pn\mathcal P_nPn​, and all of them lie in the same compact family L∘DM(1,1)\mathcal L\circ\mathcal{DM}(1,1)L∘DM(1,1). □(X,Y)≤(N+M) dconc(X,Y) \Box(X,Y)\leq(N+M)\,d_{\mathrm{conc}}(X,Y) □(X,Y)≤(N+M)dconc​(X,Y)

(Proposition 6.8). The reverse direction, deducing convergence in dconcd_{\mathrm{conc}}dconc​ from convergence of finite bounded observations, is the work of Section 6 of v3 and holds under T⊂L\mathcal T\subset\mathcal LT⊂L alone. The paper shows two things. One is that if DM(Xn;N)\mathcal{DM}(X_n;N)DM(Xn​;N) (without clipping) converges for each NNN, then XnX_nXn​ concentrates to XXX (Proposition 6.24); estimates of covering numbers and capacities of the feature family guarantee that finitely many observations approximate all features (Lemmas 6.20 and 6.21). The other is that convergence of clipped observations returns to convergence of the observations before clipping (Proposition 6.26); here an estimate on observable diameter guarantees that the values of each feature lie in a bounded range with most of the probability (Lemma 6.25). Combined, these give Theorem 6.27, a topological embedding of (D/L,dconc)(\mathcal D/\mathcal L,d_{\mathrm{conc}})(D/L,dconc​) into the stair space. This page uses that theorem as a background result and does not reproduce its proof. The finite bounded observations of PX\mathcal P_XPX​ coincide with those of SX\mathcal S_XSX​, and ρ(PX,PY)\rho(\mathcal P_X,\mathcal P_Y)ρ(PX​,PY​) is given by the same formula as the stair-space distance dΣ(SX,SY)d_\Sigma(\mathcal S_X,\mathcal S_Y)dΣ​(SX​,SY​). Theorem 6.27 therefore reads directly as the statement that Xn→XX_n\to XXn​→X is equivalent to ρ(PXn,PX)→0\rho(\mathcal P_{X_n},\mathcal P_X)\to0ρ(PXn​​,PX​)→0. Proposition 7.2 restates this in the language of weak convergence of pyramids.

Density. Let P∈ΠL\mathcal P\in\Pi_{\mathcal L}P∈ΠL​. Since (D/L,□)(\mathcal D/\mathcal L,\Box)(D/L,□) is separable, P\mathcal PP has a countable dense sequence Y1,Y2,…Y_1,Y_2,\ldotsY1​,Y2​,…. Conversely, the limit of PZn⊂P\mathcal P_{Z_n}\subset\mathcal PPZn​​⊂P stays in P\mathcal PP because P\mathcal PP is closed. Hence PZn\mathcal P_{Z_n}PZn​​ converges weakly to P\mathcal PP, and the image is dense.

Result | When all 1-Lipschitz functions are allowed, the observable diameter satisfies a limit formula on pyramids

The compactification gave limits of pyramids to sequences that do not converge. The next question is whether quantities can be read off from such a limit. Here we take the observable diameter, which measures how strongly data concentrate.

For a probability measure ν\nuν on the real line and 0<κ<10<\kappa<10<κ<1, the partial diameter is the smallest width of a set retaining probability at least 1−κ1-\kappa1−κ (Definition 2.19; the paper writes pd⁡\operatorname{pd}pd):

PartDiam⁡(ν;1−κ)=inf⁡{diam⁡I∣I⊂R is Borel, ν(I)≥1−κ}. \operatorname{PartDiam}(\nu;1-\kappa)=\inf\{\operatorname{diam}I\mid I\subset\mathbb R\text{ is Borel},\ \nu(I)\geq1-\kappa\}. PartDiam(ν;1−κ)=inf{diamI∣I⊂R is Borel, ν(I)≥1−κ}.

ObsDiam⁡(X;−κ)=sup⁡f∈FXPartDiam⁡(f∗μX;1−κ),ObsDiam⁡(E;−κ)=sup⁡X∈EObsDiam⁡(X;−κ) \operatorname{ObsDiam}(X;-\kappa)=\sup_{f\in F_X}\operatorname{PartDiam}(f_*\mu_X;1-\kappa),\qquad \operatorname{ObsDiam}(\mathcal E;-\kappa)=\sup_{X\in\mathcal E}\operatorname{ObsDiam}(X;-\kappa) ObsDiam(X;−κ)=f∈FX​sup​PartDiam(f∗​μX​;1−κ),ObsDiam(E;−κ)=X∈Esup​ObsDiam(X;−κ)

For every allowed observation we measure the width containing most of the probability, and take the largest. The observable diameter is nonincreasing and right-continuous in κ\kappaκ (Lemmas 2.20 and 2.22, Proposition 6.14), and Y⪯XY\preceq XY⪯X implies ObsDiam⁡(Y;−κ)≤ObsDiam⁡(X;−κ)\operatorname{ObsDiam}(Y;-\kappa)\leq\operatorname{ObsDiam}(X;-\kappa)ObsDiam(Y;−κ)≤ObsDiam(X;−κ) (Proposition 2.23). Proof | Extractability guarantees that passing to bounded observations loses no partial diameter

Corollary 7.7 is about the limit of observable diameters, and its proof starts from convergence of pyramids, that is, convergence of the finite bounded observations DM(⋅;N,N)\mathcal{DM}(\cdot;N,N)DM(⋅;N,N). But the observable diameter is a supremum over all features, and a feature that makes the width large may fall outside the frame of bounded observations. What we need is a guarantee that replacing each feature by one with bounded range loses, up to a small error, nothing of min⁡{r,partial diameter}\min\{r,\text{partial diameter}\}min{r,partial diameter}. The paper calls this "extractability".

Extractability. On an open interval (a,b)⊂(0,1)(a,b)\subset(0,1)(a,b)⊂(0,1), L\mathcal LL is extractable if there is a function φ ⁣:(a,b)×[0,∞)→[0,∞)\varphi\colon(a,b)\times[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)φ:(a,b)×[0,∞)→[0,∞) (an extraction estimate) such that for every Borel probability measure μ\muμ, every κ∈(a,b)\kappa\in(a,b)κ∈(a,b), every ε∈(0,b−κ)\varepsilon\in(0,b-\kappa)ε∈(0,b−κ) and every r>0r>0r>0, some g∈Lg\in\mathcal Lg∈L satisfies

min⁡{r,PartDiam⁡(μ;1−(κ+ε))}≤PartDiam⁡((bφ(κ,r))∗g∗μ; 1−κ)+2ε \min\{r,\operatorname{PartDiam}(\mu;1-(\kappa+\varepsilon))\} \leq\operatorname{PartDiam}\bigl((b_{\varphi(\kappa,r)})_*g_*\mu;\,1-\kappa\bigr)+2\varepsilon min{r,PartDiam(μ;1−(κ+ε))}≤PartDiam((bφ(κ,r)​)∗​g∗​μ;1−κ)+2ε

(Definition 6.15). The left side is the width retaining probability 1−(κ+ε)1-(\kappa+\varepsilon)1−(κ+ε), capped at rrr. The right side is the width retaining probability 1−κ1-\kappa1−κ for the measure processed by ggg and clipped to [−φ,φ][-\varphi,\varphi][−φ,φ], plus 2ε2\varepsilon2ε. The guarantee is that if we concede an extra probability ε\varepsilonε, widths up to rrr remain visible within a bounded range.

For L=Lip⁡1(R)\mathcal L=\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)L=Lip1​(R) the basis is a result of an earlier paper [10], used here as a background result.

Lemma 7.5 ([10, Theorem 1.2]). Let α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1)α∈(0,1) and R>0R>0R>0, and let μ\muμ be a Borel probability measure on R\mathbb RR. Then there is g∈Lip⁡1(R)g\in\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)g∈Lip1​(R) with values in [−R/α,R/α][-R/\alpha,R/\alpha][−R/α,R/α] such that PartDiam⁡(g∗μ;α)=min⁡{R,PartDiam⁡(μ;α)}\operatorname{PartDiam}(g_*\mu;\alpha)=\min\{R,\operatorname{PartDiam}(\mu;\alpha)\}PartDiam(g∗​μ;α)=min{R,PartDiam(μ;α)}.

Taking α=1−κ\alpha=1-\kappaα=1−κ and R=rR=rR=r, the function φ(κ,r)=r/(1−κ)\varphi(\kappa,r)=r/(1-\kappa)φ(κ,r)=r/(1−κ) is an extraction estimate. Since PartDiam⁡(μ;1−(κ+ε))≤PartDiam⁡(μ;1−κ)\operatorname{PartDiam}(\mu;1-(\kappa+\varepsilon))\leq\operatorname{PartDiam}(\mu;1-\kappa)PartDiam(μ;1−(κ+ε))≤PartDiam(μ;1−κ), the equality of Lemma 7.5 gives the inequality directly. Hence Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R) is extractable on (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) (Proposition 7.6).

Transfer and limit. Extractability is used for the following estimate: if the finite bounded observations of two closed sets E,G⊂D/L\mathcal E,\mathcal G\subset\mathcal D/\mathcal LE,G⊂D/L are close, then their observable diameters are close (Proposition 6.18). Applying it to Pn\mathcal P_nPn​ and P\mathcal PP gives the formula (Proposition 6.19). By Proposition 7.2, weak convergence of pyramids is equivalent to convergence of DM(Pn;N,N)\mathcal{DM}(\mathcal P_n;N,N)DM(Pn​;N,N), so for Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R) Corollary 7.7 follows.

Application | Data whose features are only distance functions also fit the compactification, without changing observable diameter

Corollary 7.7 concerned the observable diameter when the features are all 1-Lipschitz functions. Computing the observable diameter by its definition takes a supremum over all 1-Lipschitz functions, which costs time exponential in the number of data points #X\#X#X (introduction). Hanika–Schneider–Stumme [4] proposed restricting the features to distance functions. In this section we check that the restricted features also fit the theory of this paper, and that the observable diameter does not change.

For an mm-space XXX, take as features only the distances x↦dX(x,y)x\mapsto d_X(x,y)x↦dX​(x,y) to points yyy:

F∘(X)={x↦dX(x,y)∣y∈X},X∘=(X,F∘(X),μX). F_\circ(X)=\{x\mapsto d_X(x,y)\mid y\in X\},\qquad X_\circ=(X,F_\circ(X),\mu_X). F∘​(X)={x↦dX​(x,y)∣y∈X},X∘​=(X,F∘​(X),μX​).

Explainer's note. This is a GDS. By the triangle inequality sup⁡y∣dX(x,y)−dX(x′,y)∣\sup_y|d_X(x,y)-d_X(x',y)|supy​∣dX​(x,y)−dX​(x′,y)∣ is at most dX(x,x′)d_X(x,x')dX​(x,x′), with equality at y=x′y=x'y=x′, so it equals dX(x,x′)d_X(x,x')dX​(x,x′). For finite XXX, ObsDiam⁡(X∘;−κ)\operatorname{ObsDiam}(X_\circ;-\kappa)ObsDiam(X∘​;−κ) can be computed in O((#X)3)O((\#X)^3)O((#X)3) time (Hanika–Schneider–Stumme [4, §6.1.1]; the paper only cites this result and does not reprove it).

For a monoidal family L⊃T\mathcal L\supset\mathcal TL⊃T, write the GDS whose feature family is closed under processing as

D∘L(X)=(X, L∘F∘(X), μX)=(X, {x↦p(dX(x,y))∣p∈L, y∈X}, μX). \mathcal D_\circ^{\mathcal L}(X)=\bigl(X,\ \mathcal L\circ F_\circ(X),\ \mu_X\bigr) =\bigl(X,\ \{x\mapsto p(d_X(x,y))\mid p\in\mathcal L,\ y\in X\},\ \mu_X\bigr). D∘L​(X)=(X, L∘F∘​(X), μX​)=(X, {x↦p(dX​(x,y))∣p∈L, y∈X}, μX​).

Corollary 8.1, Proposition 8.2, Corollary 8.3. Suppose T⊂L\mathcal T\subset\mathcal LT⊂L.

  1. For every mm-space XXX, D∘L(X)\mathcal D_\circ^{\mathcal L}(X)D∘L​(X) is L\mathcal LL-compact.
  2. For every κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1)κ∈(0,1), ObsDiam⁡(D∘L(X);−κ)=ObsDiam⁡(X∘;−κ)\operatorname{ObsDiam}(\mathcal D_\circ^{\mathcal L}(X);-\kappa)=\operatorname{ObsDiam}(X_\circ;-\kappa)ObsDiam(D∘L​(X);−κ)=ObsDiam(X∘​;−κ).
  3. If TB⊂L\mathcal{TB}\subset\mathcal LTB⊂L, then the closure with respect to ρ\rhoρ of {PD∘L(X)∣X an isomorphism class of mm-spaces}\{\mathcal P_{\mathcal D_\circ^{\mathcal L}(X)}\mid X\text{ an isomorphism class of mm-spaces}\}{PD∘L​(X)​∣X an isomorphism class of mm-spaces} is a compactification of {D∘L(X)∣X an isomorphism class of mm-spaces}\{\mathcal D_\circ^{\mathcal L}(X)\mid X\text{ an isomorphism class of mm-spaces}\}{D∘L​(X)∣X an isomorphism class of mm-spaces} viewed with dconcd_{\mathrm{conc}}dconc​.

Item 1 reduces to Theorem 3.19: the metric coincides with dXd_XdX​ so that we have a GDS (the same computation as in the note above), and the processed feature family is L\mathcal LL-closed. Item 2 is short. The identity belongs to L\mathcal LL, so the original features F∘(X)F_\circ(X)F∘​(X) remain after processing, and "≥\geq≥" holds. For the converse, a 1-Lipschitz ppp does not increase the width of a set of reals, so PartDiam⁡(p∗ν;1−κ)≤PartDiam⁡(ν;1−κ)\operatorname{PartDiam}(p_*\nu;1-\kappa)\leq\operatorname{PartDiam}(\nu;1-\kappa)PartDiam(p∗​ν;1−κ)≤PartDiam(ν;1−κ), and adding features does not make the observable diameter larger. Item 3 follows because D∘L(X)∈D/L\mathcal D_\circ^{\mathcal L}(X)\in\mathcal D/\mathcal LD∘L​(X)∈D/L, so we only take a closure inside ΠL\Pi_{\mathcal L}ΠL​. If L=Lip⁡1(R)\mathcal L=\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)L=Lip1​(R), Corollary 7.7 can be used on this closure.

What is preserved is the observable diameter of X∘X_\circX∘​, whose features are chosen to be distance functions. It is not asserted to equal the observable diameter of the original mm-space with all 1-Lipschitz features. The corollary also does not claim that the limiting pyramid can be constructed in finite time.

L=Lip⁡1(R)\mathcal L=\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)L=Lip1​(R)Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R)limit formula for the observable diameter of Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R)-pyramids (Corollary 7.7)

Without clipping. The hypothesis TB⊂L\mathcal{TB}\subset\mathcal LTB⊂L in the third row is essential. Take L=T\mathcal L=\mathcal TL=T, let Xn={0,n}X_n=\{0,n\}Xn​={0,n} carry the normalized counting measure, and let the features be the restrictions of {t↦t+c}\{t\mapsto t+c\}{t↦t+c} (Remark 5.9). Every feature separates the values at the two points by exactly nnn. Observations coarsened by dropping features also keep this width, so P(Xn;T)={Xn}\mathcal P(X_n;\mathcal T)=\{X_n\}P(Xn​;T)={Xn​}. On the other hand ObsDiam⁡(Xn;−2/5)=n→∞\operatorname{ObsDiam}(X_n;-2/5)=n\to\inftyObsDiam(Xn​;−2/5)=n→∞, so if a weak limit P\mathcal PP were nonempty, its element XXX would have finite observable diameter, contradicting Proposition 2.24. Therefore the weak limit is empty.

The earlier explainer's example treated the sequence EnE_nEn​ of the same form for Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R), and its limit was the nonempty P∞\mathcal P_\inftyP∞​. In Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R), the observations EtE_tEt​ (t≤nt\leq nt≤n) whose width is shrunk by clipping lie in PEn\mathcal P_{E_n}PEn​​, whereas T\mathcal TT alone cannot shrink the width. Remark 7.4 gives another example, with T\mathcal TT, in which ιL\iota_{\mathcal L}ιL​ fails to be a topological embedding.

The stair space. When only T⊂L\mathcal T\subset\mathcal LT⊂L holds, the paper introduces a space Σ\SigmaΣ by lining up the closures S(N)\mathcal S(N)S(N) of the finite bounded observations for each NNN and imposing compatibility between levels (compatibility of measurements and directedness) (Definitions 6.1 and 6.2). The space Σ\SigmaΣ is always compact (Proposition 6.7), and (D/L,dconc)(\mathcal D/\mathcal L,d_{\mathrm{conc}})(D/L,dconc​) embeds topologically into it (Theorem 6.27). Version v3 leaves the density of this image as an open problem. The introductions of v1 and v2 stated that this embedding is "not necessarily dense" ("not dense" in the table). The statements differ between versions, and this page follows v3.

Range of the formula. Corollary 7.7 is a theorem for Lip⁡1(R)\operatorname{Lip}_1(\mathbb R)Lip1​(R). For families containing only translations, extractability is established on the interval (0,1/2)(0,1/2)(0,1/2) (Proposition 6.17, [10, Lemma 4.1]). After aligning the Lévy mean Lm(μ)\mathrm{Lm}(\mu)Lm(μ) to 000 and then clipping, any interval of probability greater than 1/21/21/2 must contain 000, so if the width is smaller than the clipping width, clipping does not change it (Lemma 6.16). On the side κ≥1/2\kappa\geq1/2κ≥1/2, where the probability can be 1/21/21/2 or less, this argument is unavailable and extractability has not been shown.

Sources | Where the page corresponds to the paper and to prior work

The central source is Yokota, the full text of arXiv:2603.23325v3. The items on this page correspond to the following places.

  • Definitions of GDS, observable distance, box distance and observable diameter: §2 (Definition 2.13, 2.16, Theorem 2.25, Proposition 2.29, Definition 2.19).
  • L\mathcal LL-compactness: §3 (Definition 3.5, Remark 3.6, Proposition 3.7, Theorem 3.19).
  • Completeness and separability: §4 (Theorem 4.10, Lemmas 4.5, 4.8, 4.9).
  • Pyramids: §5 (Definition 5.1, Theorems 5.7 and 5.8, Remark 5.9).
  • The stair space and extractability: §6 (Definition 6.1, Proposition 6.8, Definition 6.15, Propositions 6.18 and 6.19, Theorem 6.27).
  • Compactification and the limit formula: §7 (Proposition 7.2, Proposition 7.3, Remark 7.4, Lemma 7.5, Corollary 7.7).
  • Application to data whose features are distance functions: §8 (Corollary 8.1, Proposition 8.2, Corollary 8.3).

Among the prior works that the paper cites directly, the following are referred to on this page. The definition of GDS and the complexity of the observable diameter correspond to Hanika, Schneider, Stumme, Intrinsic dimension of geometric data sets, Tohoku Math. J. (2) 74 (2022), 23–52 (arXiv:1801.07985; reference [4] of v3). The extension of observable distance and box distance to GDSs, non-separability, and background results such as quotient GDSs correspond to GDS I (arXiv:2603.23316, reference [9]). Lemma 7.5 and Proposition 6.17 are Theorem 1.2 and Lemma 4.1 of Yokota, A complete proof of the limit formula for observable diameter (arXiv:2407.08122, reference [10]). Lemmas 2.20 and 2.21 on observable diameter correspond to Ozawa–Shioya, Limit formulas for metric measure invariants and phase transition property, Math. Z. 280 (2015), 759–782 (reference [6]). Lemma 2.11 rests on Beer's book (reference [1]), and the lemma on Prokhorov distance on Shioya's Metric Measure Geometry (reference [8]). The background on mm-spaces and pyramids is Gromov (reference [3]), and the motivation for discussing the dimension of data through observable diameter is Pestov (reference [7]).

This page does not reproduce the proofs of Section 6 of v3 (the stair space), the results of GDS I, the proof of Lemma 7.5, or the proof of the Hanika–Schneider–Stumme complexity bound. Nor does it treat any algorithm that constructs a limiting pyramid in finite time.

References

The numbering is that of the reference list of v3. After each entry, a note says what the paper takes from the work and where this page uses it.

  • [1] G. Beer, Topologies on Closed and Closed Convex Sets, Mathematics and its Applications 268, Kluwer, 1993. The paper quotes Theorem 5.2.12 (every sequence of closed sets in a complete separable metric space has a weakly Hausdorff convergent subsequence) as Lemma 2.11; it gives convergent subsequences of pyramids.
  • [2] D. L. Cohn, Measure Theory, 2nd ed., Birkhäuser, 2013. The paper uses Theorem 17.11 (Strassen's theorem: if dP(μ,ν)<εd_{\mathrm P}(\mu,\nu)<\varepsilondP​(μ,ν)<ε, there is a coupling giving probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon1−ε to pairs at distance at most ε\varepsilonε) to compare measures on cubes with GDS (Lemma 4.5).
  • [3] M. Gromov, Metric Structures for Riemannian and Non-Riemannian Spaces, Modern Birkhäuser Classics, English ed., 2007. Introduces mm-spaces, the observable and box distances, pyramids and the compactification of the space of mm-spaces by pyramids (Chapter 3123\frac12321​). The GDS pyramids of the paper are modelled on these; the paper cites the book only as background.
  • [4] T. Hanika, F. M. Schneider, G. Stumme, Intrinsic dimension of geometric data sets, Tohoku Math. J. (2) 74 (2022), 23–52 (arXiv:1801.07985). The paper takes from it the definition of GDS (Definition 3.2), the feature order and domination (Definition 3.4) and the observable distance (Definition 2.4). It also proposes the GDS X∘X_\circX∘​ whose features are the distance functions and shows that its observable diameter is computable in O((#X)3)O((\#X)^3)O((#X)3) time for finite XXX (§6.1.1), which Section 8 of the paper uses.
  • [5] H. Nakajima, Box distance and observable distance via optimal transport, arXiv:2204.04893, 2022. The paper borrows only Lemma 3.9: if closed sets SnS_nSn​ converge to SSS in the weak Hausdorff sense, then μ(S)≥lim sup⁡nμ(Sn)\mu(S)\ge\limsup_n\mu(S_n)μ(S)≥limsupn​μ(Sn​).

The paper borrows the right continuity of κ↦PartDiam⁡(μ;1−κ)\kappa\mapsto\operatorname{PartDiam}(\mu;1-\kappa)κ↦PartDiam(μ;1−κ) (Lemma 3.1(1)) and the comparison PartDiam⁡(μ;1−(κ+ε))≤PartDiam⁡(ν;1−κ)+2ε\operatorname{PartDiam}(\mu;1-(\kappa+\varepsilon))\le\operatorname{PartDiam}(\nu;1-\kappa)+2\varepsilonPartDiam(μ;1−(κ+ε))≤PartDiam(ν;1−κ)+2ε for dP(μ,ν)<εd_{\mathrm P}(\mu,\nu)<\varepsilondP​(μ,ν)<ε (Lemma 3.8).   • [7] V. Pestov, An axiomatic approach to intrinsic dimension of a dataset, Neural Networks 21 (2008), 204–213 (arXiv:0712.2063). Describes the curse of dimensionality as concentration of measure and proposes the observable diameter as a measure of intrinsic dimension; the computation over all 1-Lipschitz functions is exponential in the sample size, and he proposes restricting the function family. This motivates the paper.
  • [8] T. Shioya, Metric Measure Geometry, IRMA Lectures in Mathematics and Theoretical Physics 25, EMS, 2016. The paper borrows the compactness of the probability measures on [−R,R]N[-R,R]^N[−R,R]N in the Prokhorov metric (Definition 5.37, Lemma 1.17(3)), the bound of the Prokhorov distance by the Ky Fan metric (Lemma 1.26) and a covering-number comparison modelled on Lemma 3.2.

The preceding paper: the observable distance on GDS is not separable, and the box distance extended to GDS is complete but not separable. v3 uses many of its results: pointwise and in-measure convergence coincide (Lemma 2.5), Ky Fan compactness of bounded 1-Lipschitz families (Lemma 2.6), both distances are attained as minima over couplings, dconc≤□d_{\mathrm{conc}}\le\Boxdconc​≤□, domination passes to limits (Theorem 2.18), continuity of the observable diameter, and existence and uniqueness of quotient GDS.
